problem: Two different sizing rules are given for the same MCB. Section 1 says I_b ≤ I_n ≤ I_z. Section 2 says I_n ≥ 1.25 × I. A student does not know whether the 25 % margin is already inside I_b (which includes the diversity factor D) or is a separate step, and applying 1.25 to I_b gives a different answer from applying it to the plain load current.
fix: State the rule once and clearly. Example: 'Find the design current I_b = (D × ΣP)/V. Then choose I_n so that 1.25 × I_b ≥ I_n ≥ I_b and I_n ≤ I_z.' Say plainly that the 1.25 factor is the extra margin on top of the diversity-reduced design current.

problem: 'The RCCB is the only device that reacts to current leaking to earth' is too strong. When the earth path is healthy and the fault current is large, the MCB also trips on that earth-fault current, as the Q6 answer itself implies ('no fault current flows, so the MCB or RCCB may not trip').
fix: 'The RCCB is the only device that detects residual current, that is, a small leakage to earth too small to trip an MCB. A large earth-fault current may also trip the MCB as an overcurrent.'

problem: Calling an ELCB simply 'the older name' for an RCCB is imprecise. The current-operated ELCB is essentially an RCCB, but the older voltage-operated ELCB is a different device that senses the voltage of the metal body to earth and needs its own earth electrode.
fix: 'The current-operated ELCB is an older form of the same idea; the older voltage-operated ELCB works differently, sensing body-to-earth voltage, and is no longer used in homes.'

problem: 'An open earth makes the metal body live' is incomplete. A broken earth by itself does not energise the body; the body becomes live only when a fault or leakage puts live voltage on it and there is no earth path to carry the current away.
fix: 'If the earth path is open and a fault occurs, the metal body stays at live potential and no fault current flows, so neither the MCB nor the RCCB may trip.'

problem: The question adds lamps, fans, a geyser and an air conditioner and asks for one MCB. In a real board these are separate sub-circuits (5 A light circuit, 16 A power circuits), and one 16 A MCB cannot feed all of them. The answer also skips the 1.25 margin step that Q4 and Section 2 use, so the method shown differs from the rest of the chapter. The numerical result (16 A) stays correct either way.
fix: Add to the question: 'This is a load-calculation exercise; in practice each group is a separate sub-circuit.' Show the margin step: 1.25 × 11.56 A = 14.45 A, so the next standard rating is 16 A.

problem: 'Can be miswired' is vague. The real danger with a rewirable fuse is that it is rewired with a thicker wire than its rating, so it no longer protects the cable.
fix: 'It is cheap but slow, and it is often rewired with a thicker wire than the rated size, which defeats the protection.'
